newsitem.title: USA: Texas snowstorm to have limited impact on cattle.
newsitem.headline: Texas snowstorm to have limited impact on cattle.

text.p: Friday's freezing cold, heavy rain, wind and snow in the Texas Panhandle were expected to cause limited problems at feedlots, but the precipitation should boost grazing conditions, cattle sources said.

"If you have cattle out on pasture or native grass, this will mean that we are going to have fantastic spring (grazing) conditions," said C.C. Burgess, president of the Texas and Southwest Cattle Raisers Association.
"For the individuals who have cattle on feedlots, these feedlots are muddy and boggy and pretty unpleasant conditions for them at this time," Burgess said.
"When there's mud like this in the feedlot, cattle do not gain well, their efficiencies are not there and so the cost per pound of gain for the operator goes up dramatically," Burgess said.
Several feedlot sources said cattle in feedyards with snow and rain were bunched up to protect themselves from strong winds and staying away from feed bunks.

""It will take a few days for the cattle that were market ready to recover, but it shouldn't have an impact on prices next week because the stormy conditions were not widespread enough," one Panhandle feedlot manager said.

Heavy rain overnight in the Panhandle area turned to snow, with up to three inches of heavy, wet snow in Amarillo and up to five inches reported 40 miles west of the city. Temperatures in Amarillo dipped to 32 degrees Fahrenheit, a record low for the date.
"We had two inches of rain, with snow on top in our rain gauge this morning, " one feedlot source near Amarillo said.
Once temperatures rise by Sunday, feedlots will be able to clean up and get back to normal, Texas cattlemen said.
The surprise storm also was not expected to have much impact on cows still calving because temperatures were not much below freezing, Burgess said.
"If it were really cold, it would have a very negative impact on cows trying to have calves," he said.
Calving in the Texas Panhandle was about 70 percent complete, Burgess said.
The storm system now in the Texas Panhandle and western Oklahoma was seen moving to Arkansas and northern Louisiana late Saturday and early Sunday, Weather Services Corp said.
